# Interlude · When news outran the traveller {.unnumbered}

For almost all of history, news moved no faster than the people who carried it. Even the Roman state's most urgent dispatches, carried by relays of horses, managed about 250 km a day [@building-orbis-historical]. That is the speed of a rider, not of a signal, and it set the pace of every war, market, and government until the end of the eighteenth century.

The break came in France in 1794. Claude Chappe's optical telegraph passed coded signals along a chain of towers 5 to 15 km apart, each reading its neighbour through a telescope [@chappe-telegraph]. The first line ran 230 km from Paris to Lille through fifteen towers and could carry a short message in about nine minutes [@chappe-telegraph]. In August 1794 it brought the National Convention news of the recapture of Le Quesnoy and Condé-sur-l'Escaut from the Austrians within minutes [@chappe-telegraph]. A message that took four days by horse from Strasbourg now took two hours [@chappe-telegraph]. From this moment, in France at least, information travelled faster than any human could.

## What it changed

At first the telegraph served only the state. Chappe sold it as the answer to those who thought France too large to govern as a republic: it would, he argued, bring the whole country within reach of a single centre [@chappe-telegraph]. The network grew from Paris outwards, reaching Strasbourg in 1798 and Brest in 1799; by 1844 it had 534 towers linking 29 cities over more than 5,000 km, and lines ran as far as Amsterdam, Mainz, and Venice [@chappe-telegraph].

Fast news was also worth money, and the first abuses followed. Between 1834 and 1836, two Bordeaux bankers, François and Louis-Joseph Blanc, bribed telegraph operators to slip Paris stock-market movements into official messages, so they knew prices before anyone else in Bordeaux [@chappe-telegraph]. They were acquitted because no law forbade it, though fined for the bribery [@chappe-telegraph]. Alexandre Dumas made the same trick a weapon in *The Count of Monte Cristo* [@chappe-telegraph].

The electric telegraph, introduced in France from 1845, soon made the towers obsolete; the last Chappe signal was sent in 1854 [@chappe-telegraph]. Electricity also let news cross the sea, which towers never could.

## A battle fought after the peace

The cost of slow news was highest across the oceans, where no tower could reach. On 24 December 1814, British and American negotiators in Ghent, in Flanders, signed the treaty ending the War of 1812 [@new-orleans-chalmette]. Nobody in America knew. Two weeks later, on 8 January 1815, a British army of about 8,000 men attacked Andrew Jackson's 5,700 defenders just below New Orleans [@new-orleans-chalmette].

The assault collapsed in under thirty minutes. The British suffered about 2,000 casualties, including their commander, Sir Edward Pakenham; the Americans lost 71 [@new-orleans-chalmette]. Strictly, the war was not yet over: the treaty only took effect once both governments ratified it, which the US Senate did on 16 February 1815 [@new-orleans-chalmette]. But neither army even knew a treaty had been signed.

Slow news changed more than the casualty lists. The victory made Jackson a national hero, 8 January became one of only three American national holidays for the next half century, and thirteen years later Jackson was elected president [@new-orleans-chalmette]. With a telegraph cable, the battle would probably never have been fought.

## The ocean closes

Until 1866, news between Europe and America travelled by steamship, about ten days on average [@trade-impact-transatlantic]. On 30 September 1865, the price of American cotton jumped in Liverpool. Nothing moved in New York until 9 October, when a ship finally arrived with the news [@trade-impact-transatlantic].

The first durable transatlantic cable came into full operation on 28 July 1866, and communication between the continents became almost instant [@trade-impact-transatlantic]. Prices for the same cotton in New York and Liverpool drew closer and fluctuated far less. One study puts the gain at about 8 per cent of the annual value of cotton exports, as if a 6 per cent tariff had been abolished [@trade-impact-transatlantic].

From then on, this book's maps describe people and goods, not news. In 1914 a Parisian still needed six and a half days to reach New York, but word of anything that happened there arrived the same day.
